displayQuote: Money is gold, and nothing else

meta.title: Who really said "Money is gold, and nothing else"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: J. P. Morgan said it under oath before the Pujo Committee on 19 Dec 1912 — page 1081 of the official transcript. The gold-is-money version is a misquote.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Money is gold, and nothing else'?
meta.ogDescription: He said it under oath at the Pujo Committee on 19 Dec 1912; page 1081 of the transcript proves it. What he never said: Gold is money, everything else is credit.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Confirmed word for word in the government’s own record. Under cross-examination by Samuel Untermyer on Thursday, 19 December 1912, Morgan answered: “Not always. That is an evidence of banking, but it is not the money itself. Money is gold, and nothing else.” It sits on page 1081 of Money Trust Investigation, Part 15 (Government Printing Office, 1913). The version people actually share — “Gold is money. Everything else is credit.” — is nowhere in that transcript.

source.heading: The transcript, page 1081

docMeta.dd: Money Trust Investigation … under House Resolutions Nos. 429 and 504, Part 15
Washington, D.C., Thursday, 19 December 1912 — testimony of Mr. J. Pierpont Morgan, continued
1081, under cross-examination by Samuel Untermyer, counsel for the committee

source.excerpt:
Mr. UNTERMYER. I want to ask you a few questions bearing on the subject that you have touched upon this morning, as to the control of money.
Mr. MORGAN. Yes.
Mr. UNTERMYER. The control of credit involves a control of money, does it not?
Mr. MORGAN. A control of credit? No.
Mr. UNTERMYER. You do not think so?
Mr. MORGAN. What I call money is the basis of banking.
Mr. UNTERMYER. But the basis of banking is credit, is it not?
Mr. MORGAN. Not always. That is an evidence of banking, but it is not the money itself. Money is gold, and nothing else.
Mr. UNTERMYER. Do you not know that the basis of banking all over the world is credit rather than gold?
Mr. MORGAN. It is the basis of credit, but it is not the basis of money.
trail: Wikiquote lists the sentence in its sourced section for Morgan’s 1912 Pujo Committee testimony ↗ — not in the attributed or disputed section — alongside his “the first thing is character” answer from the same cross-examination.

The word-for-word confirmation is in the government’s own record. Money Trust Investigation, Part 15 ↗ opens with the session of Thursday, 19 December 1912, and carries the exchange on page 1081; Part 14 ↗ covers the previous day, Wednesday 18 December, which is why the testimony is usually dated across both.

Quote researcher Barry Popik dates the remark to 19 December 1912 ↗ and reproduces the next morning’s New York Times front page, which reported Morgan insisting that “money is gold, and nothing else.”
A second, independent scan of the same volume — the University of Michigan copy — is readable at the Internet Archive ↗, and carries the identical wording.

author.name: J. P. Morgan
author.kicker: The man in the witness chair
author.heading: Who was J. P. Morgan?
author.bio: John Pierpont Morgan was the most powerful financier in America, the banker who assembled U.S. Steel and General Electric and who personally organised the rescue that halted the Panic of 1907. That last feat made him the obvious target when Congress went looking for a “money trust” — a private cartel supposedly controlling the nation’s credit. He spent two days in December 1912 being cross-examined about it, and died in Rome on 31 March 1913, roughly three months later.

misattribution.heading: Right man, wrong words
misattribution.intro: This is an unusual case: Morgan really did say it, and almost nobody quotes him correctly. The versions that circulate are different sentences making a different claim — and the transcript of his testimony rules every one of them out.

items.who: “Gold is money. Everything else is credit.”
items.why: This is the form used by nearly every meme, quote site and investing newsletter, but it appears nowhere in Morgan’s testimony — the phrase “everything else is credit” does not occur anywhere in the Part 15 transcript ↗. Barry Popik lists it among the modern misquotations ↗ of the 1912 remark.

items.who: “Gold and silver are money. Everything else is credit.”
items.why: Morgan never mentioned silver. The word does not appear a single time in the full text of Part 15 ↗, which contains all of his 19 December testimony. Popik files this wording, too, among the modern misquotations ↗.

Same six words, opposite sentence. Morgan was defining money, not gold. Popik notes that “‘Money is gold’ is often misquoted as ‘Gold is money’” — and his file shows the flip already in print ↗ in a 1917 book and a 1925 Chase National Bank bulletin, so this one is old rather than modern. Goldmoney likewise observes that Morgan “is often misquoted” this way ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: What Morgan actually said, under oath on 19 December 1912, was: “Not always. That is an evidence of banking, but it is not the money itself. Money is gold, and nothing else.” It is on page 1081 of Part 15 of the Money Trust Investigation ↗.

context.heading: Why this sentence mattered
lead: By December 1912 the Pujo Committee had spent months trying to establish that a small circle of Wall Street men controlled the nation’s money and credit. Morgan was the star witness, and Samuel Untermyer — the committee’s counsel and the investigation’s loudest champion — cross-examined him across two days, 18 and 19 December, in a packed marble hearing room.

The famous line came out of Untermyer trying to walk Morgan into an admission: if you control credit, you control money. Morgan refused the premise flat. Credit, he said, was evidence of banking, not the thing itself — and the thing itself was gold. It was not a gold-bug slogan; it was an old banker declining to accept the question’s framing, in a hearing whose findings helped produce the Federal Reserve Act eleven months later.
context.detailsSummary: The other famous answer from the same cross-examination
detailsBody: Three pages later in the same transcript (p. 1084), Untermyer pressed Morgan on what commercial credit really rests on. Morgan: “No, sir; the first thing is character.” Untermyer: “Before money or property?” Morgan: “Before money or anything else. Money can not buy it.” He added that “a man I do not trust could not get money from me on all the bonds in Christendom.”

The two answers are often quoted as if they contradict each other — money is gold, but credit is character. Read in sequence they do not: Morgan was drawing a line between money (a settlement asset, which he said was gold) and credit (a judgment about a person). Untermyer spent the rest of the session pointing out that the world’s gold supply came nowhere near covering outstanding credit; Morgan agreed it did not.
context.pull: Before money or anything else. Money can not buy it.

sourcesVerified.claim: Money Trust Investigation, Part 15 (GPO, 1913) records the session of Washington, D.C., Thursday, December 19, 1912, and contains on page 1081 Morgan's answer: "Not always. That is an evidence of banking, but it is not the money itself. Money is gold, and nothing else."
The phrases "everything else is credit" and "gold is money", and the word "silver", do not appear anywhere in the Part 15 transcript of Morgan's testimony.

Page 1084 of the same Part 15 transcript records: "Mr. MORGAN. No, sir; the first thing is character." / "Mr. UNTERMYER. Before money or property?" / "Mr. MORGAN. Before money or anything else. Money can not buy it." and "a man I do not trust could not get money from me on all the bonds in Christendom."
Money Trust Investigation, Part 14 covers the session of Washington, D.C., Wednesday, December 18, 1912 — the day before the session containing the quote.
The University of Michigan scan of Money Trust Investigation Part 15 at the Internet Archive contains the line "is not the money itself. Money is gold, and nothing else."

Wikiquote lists "[Credit] is an evidence of banking, but it is not the money itself. Money is gold, and nothing else." under a sourced heading for Morgan's Testimony to the Pujo Committee (1912), not under Attributed or Disputed.

Barry Popik dates "Money is gold, and nothing else" to J. P. Morgan on December 19, 1912 at the Pujo Committee; reproduces the New York Times of 20 December 1912, p. 1 reporting the phrase; states that "'Money is gold' is often misquoted as 'Gold is money'"; and lists "Gold is money—everything else is credit" and "Gold and silver are money—everything else is credit" as modern misquotations. His file also reproduces the inverted form "gold is money, and nothing else" in Benjamin M. Anderson's The Value of Money (1917, p. 149) and "Gold is money and nothing else" in the Chase Economic Bulletin (1925, p. 15).

Wikipedia gives J. P. Morgan's dates as born April 17, 1837 and died March 31, 1913 in Rome, describes him as an "American financier and investment banker who dominated corporate finance on Wall Street throughout the Gilded Age and Progressive Era", and places his death approximately three months after the December 1912 Pujo testimony.
The Pujo Committee was a United States congressional subcommittee in 1912–1913 formed to investigate the so-called "money trust", and Samuel Untermyer came to be the committee's counsel.
Goldmoney's essay states that Morgan "is often misquoted to have said 'gold is money, and nothing else', which is also true but misses the important point."
